01.r: The nobleman summons his slaves before he leaves.
01.n: An aorist participle, literally 'having called'. Abbott-Smith's first sense is 'to call, summon', and he lists this verse under it.

02.r: Moves the story on from the setting to what the man does.
02.n: The BSB's 'Beforehand' reads a time sense into this small connective; the Greek only marks the next step.

03.r: The number of slaves he calls.

04.r: Men owned by the nobleman and answerable to him.
04.n: Abbott-Smith's sense as a noun is 'a slave', so this study renders it 'slave'; all six translations say 'servants'. In this parable they act as their owner's agents with his money.

05.n: A reflexive pronoun, 'of himself': Abbott-Smith's 'of himself, herself, itself'. It stresses that these are his own slaves.

06.r: He hands the money over to them.

08.r: Ten minas, one for each slave.

09.r: A unit of weight used as a sum of money.
09.n: Abbott-Smith calls it a Semitic word, akin to Hebrew מָנֶה and Aramaic מְנֵא, and gives its Attic value as 100 drachmae. This study renders it 'mina', not the KJV's 'pound', to keep it apart from the talent of Matthew 25:24.

10.r: Joins his instruction to the gift.

12.r: Directs his words to the slaves.

14.r: Put the money to work in business.
14.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to busy oneself', then 'to be engaged in business, esp. to trade', citing this verse; it is the word's only New Testament occurrence. In older English 'occupy' could mean to do business, which is why the KJV and Geneva read 'Occupy'.

15.r: With the next word, marks the time the trading should fill.
15.n: Literally 'in which', with 'time' understood: 'during the time in which I come'. English 'until' gives the sense.

16.r: A relative word that, with the word before, forms the phrase 'in the time that'.

18.r: His coming back from the journey.
18.n: A present tense, 'I am coming', used of a coming still ahead.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus reads ἕως, 'until', where our text has ἐν ᾧ, 'in the time that'. The KJV's 'till I come' translates ἕως; the meaning is close.
